Welcome to Professional and Personal Skill Development, the online course book for EXTN 4101, offered to students of the B.Sc.–M.Sc. (Integrated) Biotechnology programme at the College of Agriculture, Vellayani, Kerala Agricultural University.
A good degree opens the door to an interview, a fellowship or a laboratory; what happens after the door opens depends heavily on how well you can speak, write, organise, argue, manage your time and work with other people. These are the skills this course sets out to build. Each chapter corresponds to one lecture of the course and is paired with a practical session in which you put the ideas to work: a group discussion, a popular science article, a presentation, a debate, a quiz, an event, or a time management exercise.
The book is deliberately practical. Concepts are kept short, followed by checklists of what to do and what to avoid, and every chapter closes with a Chapter Summary containing fill-in-the-blank questions, short-answer questions and a quick revision list to help you prepare for the examination.

How to use this book

Read the chapter before the corresponding practical class, so that the class time can be spent practising rather than listening.
Complete the Practical assignment box in each chapter and keep the written record in your practical notebook.
Use the Chapter Summary at the end of each chapter for self-assessment. Answers to the fill-in-the-blank questions are given at the end of every chapter.

This book is based on the lecture notes of EXTN 4101 prepared by Dr. Esakkimuthu M., Department of Agricultural Extension Education, College of Agriculture, Vellayani (2021–22). The notes have been reorganised, edited and converted into an online book on the MeLON (Module for eLearning and Online Notes) platform of the College of Agriculture, Vellayani.

title: About the course
text:
How the book is organised
The nine lectures are grouped into three parts. Communication Skills brings together the lectures on group discussion, popular science writing, presentation skills and oral presentation, since all four deal with getting a message across to an audience. Competitive and Organisational Skills covers debate, quiz and event management, three activities in which students both participate and organise. Personal Effectiveness closes the book with time management, leadership and motivation.
The chapters on Presentation skills (3  Presentation skills) and Oral presentation (4  Oral presentation) are best read together: the first deals with planning, venue and delivery in general, and the second with the structure and language of a spoken presentation.

title: 1  Group discussion
text:
1.1 Importance of group discussion
Group discussion (GD) is a comprehensive technique used to judge the suitability of individuals for admission, scholarships, jobs and similar opportunities. A GD assesses the overall personality of an individual (thoughts, feelings and behaviour) while working in a group. A topic is presented to the group members for discussion, and while the discussion goes on, a panel of observers watches the participants. Through this observation the panel judges the intellectual, social, leadership and communication skills of each candidate.
Admission to many universities and business schools, campus placements after graduation, and recruitment to multinational companies all look for two things: knowledge of the field, and the ability to work in a group, either as a leader or as a member. A group discussion is a very effective way of judging the second of these, the candidate’s ability to work with others.

title: 1  Group discussion
section: 1.2 Skills judged in a group discussion

title: 1  Group discussion
text:
1.3 Components of a group discussion
Purpose
The first component is the purpose of holding the discussion. The aim of a group discussion is to arrive at a satisfactory conclusion, and a GD usually helps the group decide the next course of action.
Planning
Planning is a crucial element. A group discussion that aims to arrive at a decision cannot be a random expression of ideas; it has to be planned so that every step takes the group closer to its goal.
Participation
Participation of the members is the life of any group discussion. Every member has to be drawn into the discussion, and it should not be dominated by a few.

title: 1  Group discussion
section: 1.4 Do’s and don’ts of participating in a group discussion
text:
1.4 Do’s and don’ts of participating in a group discussion



Table 1.1: Do’s and don’ts in a group discussion









Do’s
Don’ts




Think before you speak.
Do not initiate the discussion if you do not know the topic well.


If you know little about the topic, pick up clues from the discussion and add points intelligently.
Do not go overboard in displaying your knowledge, even if you know the topic well.


Back up your points with facts and figures where needed.
Do not interrupt other members when they are speaking.


Be gentle and sure in presenting your views.
Do not change your opinion only because most of the group holds a different one.


Speak to the point and do not repeat points already made.
Do not lose confidence if an earlier speaker presented a point better than you could.


Be calm and composed while speaking.
Do not ask irrelevant questions.


Listen to others; listening is also part of participation.
Do not let your personal biases about the topic enter the discussion.


Respect the viewpoints of others.



Let your body language show that you are at ease.



If the discussion turns hostile, intervene to calm it; this shows leadership and problem-solving skill.

title: 1  Group discussion
text:
1.5 Preparing for a group discussion
Nobody knows in advance what the topic of a GD will be, so it is wise to keep yourself informed on a broad range of subjects.

Current affairs. Read newspapers regularly and follow the news. Understand the current crises facing the world, recent development initiatives, relations between countries, and similar issues.
Historical topics. Have a fair knowledge of the history of your own country and of other countries. The topic may not come directly from history, but historical information helps you cite examples and make references when needed.
Sports, arts and literature. Keep a general awareness of major events, personalities and works in these areas.
Data. Familiarise yourself with important figures and statistics. A relevant number used at the right moment creates a strong impression on the assessors.

Read as widely as possible and build sound knowledge on many topics; documentaries help here. Improve your vocabulary, not so that you can use heavy words, but so that you understand topics better and contribute effectively. Finally, picture yourself succeeding in the discussion; confidence comes from preparation.






Practical assignment



Write down the points you would raise in a group discussion on the topic “Indian education during the COVID-19 pandemic”. Organise them as an opening statement, three or four main points with supporting facts, and a concluding statement.

title: 2  Popular science articles
text:
2.1 Tips for writing a good popular science article
A popular science article is an interpretation of science intended for a general audience. Such articles aim to inform non-specialist readers about new scientific insights and discoveries. Popular science is closely related to science journalism, which focuses on recent scientific developments, and it may be written either by professional science journalists or by scientists themselves. It appears in many forms, including books, film and television documentaries, magazine articles and web pages.
For a biotechnology student, writing for the public is an important skill. Research that cannot be explained to the people who fund it, use it or are affected by it loses much of its value.
Ask the right questions
Begin ordering your ideas by asking yourself: what? where? when? how? why? and who? Once you know what you want to communicate, and why, lay out your core idea first and expand on it in the rest of the article. Always be clear about the exact purpose of what you are writing; a clear intent gives you a much better chance of producing an effective article.
Structure the article well
Know where you are going. Set up a human connection and a question at the start that carries the reader from beginning to end, rewarding them with clues along the way, and place the take-home message at the end. Readers tend to remember the beginning and the end of a piece, along with any high point in the middle, so plan those three moments carefully.
Use a catchy title
A good title excites readers and catches their attention. A popular science title should attract non-specialists and should be short. Avoid technical terms; combining a difficult term with an easy phrase can sometimes make the reader curious. For example:
Write for a non-specialist reader
In a popular science article, research results are communicated to readers who are not specialists in your topic. Assume that they have no knowledge beyond high school science, but always respect their intelligence. Give an overview of the study, provide only the most significant information, and simplify the results. Be accurate, but avoid too many details. Avoid long, flowery phrases and follow the principle of one idea per sentence.
Avoid jargon
There may be words, acronyms and abbreviations that people outside your field simply would not know. Be aware of your reader’s knowledge and choose words and phrases you are certain they will understand. If a technical term cannot be avoided, explain it the first time it appears.
Use the active voice
Where possible, use the active voice rather than the passive. The aim is to engage the reader, and active, personal language does exactly that. For example, instead of writing “the reactions of various metals were tested”, write “we tested the reactions of various metals”. Adding the word we makes the writing more personal.

title: 2  Popular science articles
text:
Membrane proteins: Saint Peter of the cells
Birds of a feather: do they always flock together?
And God said, “Let there be light”, preferably modulated light
Can you control your genes, or do your genes control you?
What has 24 eyes but no brain?

title: 2  Popular science articles
text:
2.2 Concluding advice

Make sure the content and language of the article suit a wide circle of readers.
Keep the title short and catchy.
Structure the article well.
Describe methods and techniques only briefly.
When describing results, focus on what they mean and how they can be applied.
Use as few technical terms as possible and avoid excessively long sentences.







Practical assignment



Choose a recent research finding in biotechnology and write a popular science article of about 600 to 800 words on it. Give it a catchy title, open with a human connection, and end with a clear take-home message.

title: 3  Presentation skills
text:
3.1 Why we give presentations
A presentation is a talk, usually given in a formal setting such as a business, technical, professional or scientific environment, in which something is set before an audience for their attention and understanding. Presenting is a skill developed through experience and training. The key elements of a presentation are the presenter, the audience, the message, the reaction of the audience, and the method used to deliver the message effectively.
Understanding the true purpose of a presentation helps you prepare and deliver it more effectively. Common purposes are:

title: 3  Presentation skills
text:
To teach or train. Anyone who works in a teaching role gives this kind of presentation regularly: teachers, professors, professional trainers, tour guides, podcast hosts, news anchors and many others.
To gather opinions. A presentation can be used to collect the views of an audience on a topic of interest.
To publicise an idea. Managers, consultants, freelance professionals, doctors and entrepreneurs often have an idea they want, or need, to share with others.
To share research findings. Such presentations give an overview of research carried out by an individual or a group.
To highlight a problem. A presentation can draw attention to a problem of real importance and seek a solution to it.
To pass on information. Similar to teaching, but the aim is to communicate as much information as possible in the time available. Many organisations expect students or employees to report progress at key stages of a project in this way.
To entertain. An amusing historical talk, a story or a reading can hold a crowd; entertaining an audience well is a truly artistic skill and a very rewarding one.

title: 3  Presentation skills
section: 3.2 Seven basic steps in a presentation
text:
3.2 Seven basic steps in a presentation

Decide what you want to achieve.
Decide whether a formal presentation is the best way to achieve this objective.
If you decide to go ahead, decide what form the presentation should take.
Prepare a script, in whatever form suits you best.
Design and prepare your visual aids and handouts.
Rehearse properly.
Deliver it.

title: 3  Presentation skills
text:
3.3 Skills needed for effective delivery
Enthusiasm and commitment to the topic
Believe in what you are saying, because most audiences can detect a fake almost instantly. Prepare carefully and understand the topic so well that you cannot help being enthusiastic about it. Most people would rather listen to anything presented with enthusiasm than to the most important information presented dully.
Knowledge of the topic
Understand your subject before you start speaking. Content is central to any presentation, and it must be accurate, factual and well organised.
Understanding of the audience
While preparing, always keep in mind what the audience needs and wants to know, not merely what you can tell them.
Appearing to be in control
Appear relaxed and confident. Smile and make eye contact with the audience; this builds the rapport that helps listeners connect with you and your subject.
Use of voice and body language
Varying your speed, pitch and tone makes your voice more interesting and holds the audience’s attention. A large part of communication is non-verbal, so your body language is as important as your words. Avoid crossed arms, hands held behind your back or in your pockets, and pacing up and down the stage.
A style suited to the audience and the objective
The best style depends on the subject, the audience and the way you prefer to explain the material. You may keep one style throughout, or mix styles to explain the topic better.
Handling questions with ease
If you can relax, you will almost certainly present better and handle questions more comfortably. If you actually start to enjoy yourself, the audience will respond and engage better, and your confidence will grow with every presentation.
Retaining your natural style
One of the most important factors in a successful presentation is the ability to look and act naturally. If you are stiff, uncomfortable and “not yourself”, the audience will notice and respond poorly. Refine particular elements of your delivery, but keep your own style.
Reading the mood of the audience
While presenting, stay alert to how the audience is responding, and adapt when their mood changes.

title: 3  Presentation skills
section: 3.4 Effect of the venue and seating on the audience
text:
3.4 Effect of the venue and seating on the audience
The room and its arrangement can help or hinder a presentation before the speaker says a word. Table 3.1 lists common problems and their effect on the audience.



Table 3.1: Effect of venue and seating arrangements on the audience









Venue or seating condition
Effect on the audience




Room too large
Feels inhibiting and uncomfortable; prevents building rapport; often becomes too cold


Room too small
Feels claustrophobic and awkward for lack of personal space; often becomes too hot


Room with pillars
Restricts vision


Poorly lit room
Hinders attention


Seating too close together
Uncomfortable


Members cannot see each other when speaking
Creates barriers and resentment


No tables
Awkward for anyone who wants to take notes


Room decorated with irrelevant posters and charts
Distracts attention


A hostile member seated in the centre of the speaker’s field of vision
Difficult to control; can dominate, creating resentment among other members of the audience


Speaker on a platform
A very strong, controlling position


Speaker with many notes sharing a table with the audience
Inhibiting for everyone

title: 3  Presentation skills
section: 3.5 Statements that make a presentation work
text:
3.5 Statements that make a presentation work

Presentations need clear and specific objectives.
Nerves can ruin a presenter’s confidence, so prepare well to keep them in check.
It is not what you say but the way that you say it.
Small is beautiful: a short, focused presentation often works better than a long one.
Use a “hook” at the start of the talk.
A presentation needs a beginning, a middle and an end.
The audience plays an important part in the preparation stage.
Presenters can “win” or “lose” their audience within the first few minutes.
Visual aids should enhance the presentation, not distract from it.

title: 3  Presentation skills
text:
3.6 Personal presentation

Stand at ease. Avoid settling in one spot, leaning to one side, leaning over the podium or sitting on the table.
Take care of your style of speaking: make your voice expressive and take care of your voice.
Rehearse; rehearsal is a must for efficient delivery.
Avoid the following postures:

hands on the waist, which shows arrogance;
hands in the pockets, which looks too casual;
hands behind the back, which looks authoritarian, stiff and too formal;
arms folded over the stomach, which shows a defensive attitude;
rubbing hands together, which looks fussy and possibly dishonest.

Select visual aids suited to your presentation.
Arrange the room in advance: seating plan, electronic equipment, drinking water and so on.
Stick to the time plan.
Use handouts when necessary.

title: 3  Presentation skills
section: 3.7 A three-step framework for every presentation
text:
3.7 A three-step framework for every presentation
A simple framework that works for almost every presentation is:
Step 1. Tell participants what you will cover: review the objectives and explain what they will experience (questions, a case study, a discussion and so on).
Step 2. Deliver the content and facilitate learning through activities, exercises, discussion and audience response.
Step 3. Remind the audience what you have discussed and accomplished together, and link back to your objectives.

title: 3  Presentation skills
text:
3.8 Conclusion
Presenting information clearly and effectively is a key skill in getting a message across, and the present era places great emphasis on it. Within an organisation, managers with good presentation skills are better able to communicate the mission and vision of the organisation to its employees.






Practical assignment



Prepare and deliver a short presentation on the topic assigned to you in the practical class. Attach the first assigned document (the script or slides) to your practical record.

title: 4  Oral presentation
text:
4.1 Features of an oral presentation
An oral presentation is essentially a spoken form of technical writing; it involves both the activity and the art of speaking to the public. With the spread of modern media and technology, oral presentation has become a significant means of communication for scientists, engineers and other technical personnel. The presentation situation rests on interaction between the presenter and the audience. Because it brings the listener face to face with the presenter, an oral presentation also broadens the thinking of those who wrote the underlying report or project. It is therefore important for every presenter to acquire the skills of oral presentation. This chapter builds on the general principles of Chapter 3.

title: 4  Oral presentation
text:
It is a participative, two-way communication process.
It is purposeful, interactive and audience oriented.
It communicates a message in a way that brings about the desired change in the audience’s understanding and opinion.

title: 4  Oral presentation
section: 4.2 How to make a good oral presentation
text:
4.2 How to make a good oral presentation

4.2.1 Conquering stage fright
Stage fright arises mainly because most of us are not accustomed to speaking in public. Its signs include trembling hands, excessive sweating and loss of fluency. To overcome it:

prepare the subject thoroughly;
do some warm-up exercises;
eat a healthy meal and drink enough water;
rehearse the presentation.



4.2.2 Knowing the audience
Before planning the presentation, consider:

the age group of the audience;
the needs of the audience;
the usefulness of the presentation to them;
the information they should gain after attending it.



4.2.3 Content of the presentation

It should not be too difficult to understand.
If it is too long, shorten it to fit the time available.
Include examples and illustrations to support the argument.



4.2.4 Structure of the presentation
A typical presentation has three parts: the beginning, the middle and the end (introduction, body and conclusion).
The beginning (introduction)
The beginning is the most important part of a presentation, so be confident and well prepared for it.

Greet the audience: “Hello”, “Good morning”, and so on.
Introduce yourself, for example: “Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Let me introduce myself…” or “Good morning, everyone. I’d like to start by introducing myself. My name is…”
Give the title and introduce the subject, using phrases such as “I plan to speak about…”, “Today I’m going to talk about…”, “The subject of my presentation is…”, “The theme of my talk is…” or “I’ve been asked to give you an overview of…”.
Give a brief outline of the main points you will cover.

The middle (body)

Provide detailed information about the topic.
Give clear explanations.
Provide enough evidence to be convincing.
Use analogies and stories to explain complicated ideas and to reinforce key points.

The end (conclusion)

Summarise your points.
Conclude the topic with the ideas developed in the talk.
End with “Thank you.”
If you are taking questions, tell the audience: “I’ll now be happy to answer any questions.”



4.2.5 Delivery of the presentation
Quality of voice

Adjust your volume and tone to the size of the audience.
Use a microphone or collar microphone where needed.
Pause at appropriate points.
Pronounce difficult words clearly and correctly.

Rapport with the audience

Make eye contact with the audience.
Shift your gaze from one person to another so that you take in everyone.
Involve the audience by asking questions.

Body language

Express confidence through your smile and movements.
Stand straight, and do not stay rooted to one spot.
Avoid unnecessary hand movements.
Dress formally.

Effective use of visual aids

Keep the layout pleasant and easy to read; a horizontal (landscape) layout is preferable.
Use clear fonts such as Arial, Helvetica, Times New Roman, Futura, Optima, Verdana, New Century Schoolbook or Courier. Some organisations prescribe a particular style.
Use a font size of 20 or more, depending on the size of the room. A useful scheme is 20 points for main headings, 16 for subheadings and 14 for other text.
Use capital letters, bold face, italics, underlining, reverse type (white on black) or shading to highlight key points, but sparingly.







Practical assignment



Prepare a ten-minute oral presentation with slides on a topic of your choice from biotechnology. Record the opening sentences you will use for the greeting, self-introduction and outline, and the closing sentences for the summary and invitation to questions.

title: 5  Debate
text:
5.1 Why debate?
A debate is a structured argument. Two sides speak alternately for and against a particular motion, usually based on a topical issue. Unlike the arguments you may have with family or friends, each speaker is allotted a fixed time, and any interruptions are carefully controlled. The motion is often decided in advance, so you may find yourself supporting opinions with which you do not normally agree. You also argue as part of a team, and must be careful not to contradict what others on your side have said.
Debating is an excellent way of improving speaking skills, and it is particularly useful for gaining experience in building a convincing argument. Those who are asked to argue against their natural point of view soon realise that arguments, like coins, always have at least two sides.

title: 5  Debate
text:
5.2 Basic debating skills
Debating skills fall under three heads: style, content and strategy. This chapter deals with the first two.

5.2.1 Style
Style is the manner in which you communicate your arguments. It is the most basic part of debating to master, because content and strategy are worth little unless the material is delivered in a confident and persuasive way.
Speed
Speak at a pace that is fast enough to sound intelligent and to let you say what you want, but slow enough to be easily understood.
Tone
Varying your tone is what makes you sound interesting. Listening to one tone for an entire speech is boring.
Volume
Speaking loudly is sometimes necessary, but there is no need to shout through every debate regardless of context. Speak at a volume at which everyone in the room can hear you comfortably, and no louder. Shouting does not win debates; speaking too quietly is equally disastrous, since no one will hear you.
Clarity
The ability to express complex issues clearly and concisely is what debating is all about. Speakers usually become unclear when they lose the stream of thought that keeps them going. Keep it simple: long words may make you sound clever, but they may also make you incomprehensible.
Use of notes and eye contact
Notes are essential, but they must be brief and well organised to be effective. There is no point in trying to speak without notes, but notes should never become obtrusive, damage your contact with the audience, or be read out word for word. Most speakers sketch the main headings of their speech with brief points under each.
While noting points for rebuttal during the debate, it is usually better to use a separate sheet: take down what the other speakers have said, then transfer a rough outline onto the notes you will actually use.
Eye contact with the audience is very important, but keep shifting your gaze; no one likes to be stared at.


5.2.2 Content
Content is what you actually say in the debate: the arguments used to develop your own side’s case and to rebut the other side’s. The practical details (how long each speaker has, how many members are in a team, and which team speaks first) are fixed by the teacher conducting the debate.
The case as a whole
Introduction. The case your team is making must be outlined at the start. State your main arguments and explain the general thrust of the case. Do this briefly, since the most important thing is to get on and actually argue it. It is also useful to indicate which aspects of the motion each team member will cover.
Conclusion. At the end, once everyone has spoken, briefly summarise what your team has said and why.
The case in parts
Having outlined the whole argument, build the case in parts. The best way is to divide the case into two to four arguments, or according to the number of speakers in the team. Justify each argument with logic, worked examples, statistics and quotations. Debating is all about proof: evidence supporting your assertion is what turns it into an argument.
Arguments can be grouped in several ways, for example political, economic and social; moral and practical; or international and regional. If no grouping fits, simply present individual arguments. Under each heading, explain the reasoning behind the argument and justify it with evidence. It is usually best to put the most important argument first.
An example of a case outline:

“The media exert more influence over what people think than the government does. This is true for three reasons. Firstly, most people base their votes on what they see and hear in the media. Secondly, the media can set the political agenda between elections by deciding which issues to report and in how much detail. Thirdly, the media have successfully demonised politicians over the last ten years, so that people are now more likely to believe journalists than politicians.”

Every argument in this outline is debatable (counter-arguments come to mind almost immediately), but together they give the case a wide range covering many issues. The trick is not to build a watertight case, but a well-argued one.

A debate was conducted in the practical class on the motion “The minimum legal age of marriage for women should be raised to 21 years.” Record the case outline of your team, the arguments you presented with their supporting evidence, and the main points of rebuttal from the opposing team.

title: 6  Quiz
text:
6.1 Procedure for conducting a quiz
A quiz is a game or mind sport in which players attempt to answer questions correctly on one subject or on a variety of subjects. It is a test of knowledge, usually held as a competition between individuals or teams. Questions can take many formats: single or multiple choice, fill in the blank, find the word, matching, and picture, audio or video questions.
The objective of a quiz competition is to encourage students to look beyond their textbooks and to connect the theory they have learnt with its applications. Quizzes also reveal gaps in knowledge and highlight areas that need more revision.
In education, a quiz is often a brief form of assessment used to measure growth in knowledge, abilities or skills. Compared with a formal test, a quiz usually has fewer and easier questions and takes less time to complete. A pop quiz is one given without any warning, so that students have no time to prepare.
Step 1: Know your audience
Every successful quiz is pitched at the right level for the people taking part. Find out who the participants are (school students, undergraduates, postgraduates or the general public) and what they can reasonably be expected to know.
Step 2: Choose a topic and a title
The title should be attractive, should draw in the intended audience, and should be short and to the point. However good the questions are, a dull title can keep participants away.
Step 3: Frame the questions
Keep the questions short and clear. Avoid long or complicated questions that confuse participants or make them lose interest. Mix easy and difficult questions, and arrange them in rounds of different formats to keep the quiz lively. Check every answer against a reliable source before the event.
Step 4: Plan the scoring and the results
Decide in advance how points will be awarded, whether there will be negative marking, and how ties will be broken. When announcing results, keep the tone positive so that every participant, including those who did not win, leaves feeling encouraged.
Step 5: Follow up
A quiz should lead somewhere: to further reading, a related event, or a chance for participants to learn more about the topic. In online quizzes this is called a call to action, shown to participants along with their results.
Step 6: Make it shareable
Encourage participants to share their experience and results. People share results that make them feel good or smart, so present results in an uplifting way. For online quizzes, a shareable title and attractive results help the quiz reach a wider audience.

title: 7  Event management
text:
7.1 SWOT analysis
An event can be described as a public gathering for the purpose of celebration, education, marketing or reunion. Events can be classified by size, type and context. Three broad categories are:
Event management is the process of analysing, planning, marketing, producing and evaluating an event. It is also a distinct way of promoting a product, a service or an idea: a well-managed event can be a very powerful promotional tool for launching or marketing a product or service.
SWOT analysis is a strategic planning tool used to identify and analyse the Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats involved in a project. It helps the organiser make the most of strengths and opportunities and reduce the impact of weaknesses and threats. Strengths and weaknesses are internal to the organising team; opportunities and threats come from the external environment (Table 7.1).

title: 7  Event management
text:
Table 7.1: SWOT analysis for an event











Helpful to the event’s objectives
Harmful to the event’s objectives




Internal
Strengths: experienced event team, high motivation, good market share
Weaknesses: lack of funds, inexperienced team, low energy, lack of media and corporate contacts


External
Opportunities: little competition, favourable economic conditions, support from local authorities
Threats: strong competition, bad weather, unavailability of materials, no support from local authorities

title: 7  Event management
text:
7.2 Planning with the five W’s
An event plan is built around five questions: Why, What, When, Where and Who.
Why
Why do you want to organise the event? This is the event objective: what you want to get out of it. You may want to enhance your organisation’s image, increase sales, or promote a social cause. The objective gives direction to everything else. Organising an event without clear objectives is a huge waste of time and resources.
What
What will happen at the event? This covers:

Event name: use your imagination to create a title that attracts guests.
Programme: the list of activities that will take place during the event.
Budget: the cost of producing and marketing the event.
Food and beverage menu: the food and drinks to be served.
Guest profile: the guest list, including organisers, sponsors, partners, clients and, especially, the media.

When
When will the event be held (date and time)? While choosing:

Select a date and time convenient for the target audience. Avoid working days, examination periods and festival times; weekends are usually best.
Make sure the event does not clash with other events, especially bigger ones.
Consider the likely weather conditions.

Where
Where will the event be held? The venue depends on:

the size of the expected audience;
the convenience of the audience;
the history of the venue.

The venue should comfortably hold the expected audience, being neither too small nor too large, and should not be far from where most of the audience lives.
Who
Who will be the organisers, sponsors, partners, clients and target audience? How many people do you expect to attend, and why? You need a sound answer to this “why”, because you will have to convince prospective organisers and sponsors that the expected number will actually attend.

title: 7  Event management
text:
7.3 Event marketing
An event must be advertised: to create awareness, to attract sponsors and participants, and to thank sponsors and clients afterwards. Marketing is mainly done through five kinds of media: print, electronic, outdoor, transit and miscellaneous media.

title: 7  Event management
text:
7.4 Event evaluation
Evaluation makes you more efficient and effective the next time you organise an event. It is about finding your mistakes and learning from them, and it should be done immediately after the event, for example by collecting feedback forms from participants and clients.

title: 7  Event management
text:
7.5 An overview of the process
First, analyse the event. Then prepare an event plan by studying your market, and bring together organisers, sponsors, partners and clients. Finally, prepare an event calendar: an ordered list of the activities needed to produce and market the event. These activities are of three types: pre-event, at-event and post-event.

title: 7  Event management
section: 7.6 Seven steps for perfect programme planning
text:
7.6 Seven steps for perfect programme planning
Step 1. Understand the need for a strategic plan. Assess the needs of the people the programme is meant for by listening, observing and examining data. Set priorities based on concern and importance.
Step 2. Plan. Planning is the most important stage in achieving the proposed objectives. Visualise what you want to achieve; without this you cannot measure the results or verify that the objective was achieved. Two tools help at this stage:

Logic model. A graphic representation of the programme showing what is to be invested (inputs), what is to be done (activities and outputs) and what the results will be (outcomes). It is a common framework for the work and the core of programme planning and evaluation.
SMART objectives. Learning objectives should be Specific (what exactly will you accomplish?), Measurable (how will you know you have reached it?), Achievable (is it realistic with effort and commitment?), Relevant (why is it significant to the programme?) and Time-bound (when will you achieve it?).

Step 3. Develop the programme. Select the format and draw up the programme schedule. Select and organise the content and the educational resources.
Step 4. Promote. Estimate the overall expense and take steps to obtain resources and sponsors. Prepare attractive marketing material aimed at the target audience.
Step 5. Deliver. Aim to create a positive learning experience for the audience. Practise before delivery, and work in groups with clearly assigned duties.
Step 6. Evaluate. Collect feedback from the audience.
Step 7. Communicate results. Report the outcome of the programme. Discuss every suggestion received, and put together the expenses and estimates for evaluation.






Historical Insights



The SMART acronym was introduced by George T. Doran in a 1981 article in Management Review titled “There’s a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management’s goals and objectives” (Doran 1981). In Doran’s original version, the “A” stood for assignable and the “T” for time-related; later writers changed the words, but the idea of testing every objective against five criteria remained.

title: 8  Time management
text:
8.1 The time management matrix
Time management is the process of planning and exercising conscious control over the time spent on specific activities, especially to increase effectiveness, efficiency and productivity. It helps you organise and plan how to divide your time between different activities. By learning to manage your time, you can improve your work, increase your productivity, lower your stress and build a healthy balance between work and the rest of your life.
The time management matrix is a self-management tool now widely used to prioritise important tasks and to identify time-wasters. It helps you decide which activities are important, which are urgent, and which are merely distractions or interruptions. Tasks are classified into four quadrants (Table 8.1):
Effective people try to spend most of their time in Quadrant 2. Activities in this quadrant, such as planning, preparation, building relationships and looking after one’s health, prevent many tasks from becoming urgent crises in Quadrant 1 later.

title: 8  Time management
text:
Urgent and important. Examples: the birth of your child; a customer complaint; an assignment due tomorrow.
Important but not urgent. Examples: paying your taxes; getting your vehicle serviced; calling your mother; preparing steadily for an examination.
Urgent but not important. Example: answering every e-mail within ten minutes of receiving it.
Neither urgent nor important. Examples: a binge-watching session; reading the comments under a news article.




Table 8.1: The time management matrix











Urgent
Not urgent




Important
Quadrant 1: Urgent and important (do it now)
Quadrant 2: Important but not urgent (plan and schedule it)


Not important
Quadrant 3: Urgent but not important (limit or delegate it)
Quadrant 4: Neither urgent nor important (avoid it)













Historical Insights



The matrix is often called the Eisenhower matrix, after US President Dwight D. Eisenhower. In a 1954 address he quoted a former college president: “I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important. The urgent are not important, and the important are never urgent.” The idea was popularised as a four-quadrant time management tool by Stephen R. Covey in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (Covey 1989).

title: 9  Leadership and motivation
text:
9.1 Leadership
Leadership is the ability of an individual or a group of individuals to influence and guide followers or other members of an organisation. Leaders help themselves and others to do the right things. They set direction, build an inspiring vision and create something new. Leaders are needed in almost every part of society, from business and politics to religion and community-based organisations.
Leadership means different things to different people around the world, and different things in different situations. An effective leader generally shows the following characteristics:
Leadership often requires leaders to take on some management tasks, but good leaders understand that their strengths differ from those of good managers. Managers excel at setting out the steps needed to complete tasks and at holding people accountable for their share of the work. A leader shapes and moulds the behaviour of the group towards the goals of the organisation, develops a vision of the future, and motivates members of the organisation to want to achieve that vision.

title: 9  Leadership and motivation
9  Leadership and motivation
text:
9.2 Types of leadership
Some leaders have one dominant style, while others use different styles in different situations or with different followers. Commonly identified leadership styles are described below.
Autocratic
This is the command-and-control approach. An autocratic leader believes that he or she is the smartest person at the table and knows more than others, and makes all the decisions with little input from team members.
Authoritative (visionary)
Authoritative leaders are confident leaders who map the way and set expectations while engaging and energising their followers. They help people see where the organisation is going and what will happen when it gets there. Unlike autocratic leaders, authoritative leaders take the time to explain their thinking instead of simply issuing orders. Above all, they allow people choice and freedom in how to achieve common goals.
Pacesetting
A pacesetter is a very driven leader who sets the pace, as in a race. Pacesetters set the bar high and push team members to run hard and fast to the finish line. This style is effective in getting things done and driving results, but it can wear team members down. A pacesetting leader needs to ease off from time to time to avoid burning out the team.
Democratic
Democratic leaders share with team members the information that affects their work, and seek their opinions before making a final decision. This builds trust and promotes team spirit and cooperation. It allows for creativity and helps team members grow and develop. A democratic style gets people to do what needs to be done, but in a way that they want to do it.
Coaching
A coaching leader sees people as a reservoir of talent to be developed, and seeks to unlock their potential in the belief that everyone has power within themselves. Such a leader gives people a little direction to help them achieve their full potential.
Affiliative
Of all the styles, the affiliative approach is the most personal. An affiliative leader pays attention to and supports the emotional needs of team members. The style is about encouraging harmony and building collaborative relationships within teams.
Laissez-faire
The laissez-faire style is the opposite of the autocratic style and involves the least oversight. A laissez-faire leader appears to trust people to know what to do. This style can work when leading highly skilled, experienced, self-motivated people. To make it effective, the leader should still monitor team performance and give regular feedback.
Because leadership depends on the situation, there is no single best style. The right style is the one that suits the situation the leader is facing.






Historical Insights



Six of these styles (coercive or autocratic, authoritative, affiliative, democratic, pacesetting and coaching) come from Daniel Goleman’s article “Leadership That Gets Results” in the Harvard Business Review (Goleman 2000), which linked each style to different aspects of emotional intelligence. The laissez-faire style is much older: it was one of the three “social climates” (autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire) compared by Kurt Lewin, Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White in their experiments with boys’ clubs in the late 1930s (Lewin, Lippitt, and White 1939).

title: 9  Leadership and motivation
9  Leadership and motivation
text:
9.4 Theories of motivation

9.4.1 Maslow’s hierarchy of needs
Abraham Maslow described human needs as a hierarchy (Figure 9.1). Needs at the bottom of the hierarchy must be satisfied before an individual moves to the next level and seeks to satisfy those needs (Maslow 1943). Each person’s needs keep changing, but at any given time an employer can use the hierarchy to judge what is likely to motivate an employee.
The five levels of the hierarchy are:

Physiological needs: food, water and other necessities of life.
Safety needs: freedom from war and natural disasters, and job security.
Social needs: relationships and belonging to groups.
Esteem needs: praise, recognition and status.
Self-actualisation needs: the desire to become the best one can be.







Figure 9.1: Maslow’s hierarchy of needs





9.4.2 McClelland’s three needs theory
David McClelland’s three needs theory holds that each of us has three needs, to a greater or lesser extent (McClelland 1961):

Need for achievement: for example, being motivated by setting a new record or by the chance of promotion.
Need for affiliation: for example, being motivated by working with others or by being accepted as part of a group.
Need for power: for example, being motivated by being in charge of others or by holding high status.



9.4.3 McGregor’s Theory X and Theory Y
Douglas McGregor’s Theory X and Theory Y place employees in two broad categories (McGregor 1960).

Theory X assumes that team members are inherently lazy and unmotivated, and will avoid work whenever they can. Management must therefore work continuously to build systems of control and supervision.
Theory Y assumes that team members are ambitious and self-motivated. A Theory Y manager believes that, given the right conditions, team members will perform well.



9.4.4 Herzberg’s two-factor theory
Frederick Herzberg argued that two kinds of factors determine the motivation of employees: motivators and hygiene factors (Herzberg, Mausner, and Snyderman 1959).

Motivators encourage employees to work harder when they are present. Examples include an interesting job, advancement and growth.
Hygiene factors do not encourage employees to work harder, but their absence makes employees dissatisfied and demotivated. Examples include working conditions and pay.




Table 9.1: Summary of theories of motivation










Theory
Proposed by
Central idea




Hierarchy of needs
Abraham Maslow (1943)
Five levels of needs, satisfied from the bottom up


Three needs theory
David McClelland (1961)
Needs for achievement, affiliation and power


Theory X and Theory Y
Douglas McGregor (1960)
Two opposing managerial assumptions about employees


Two-factor theory
Frederick Herzberg (1959)
Motivators drive effort; hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction
